note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — MANY ONE-SIDED RACEMES
tiles.details: New Harry Rose locally archived gallery panel 10 (index9) documents a REAL leafy Vaseygrass clump with attached many-raceme flowering culms. Original whole-head panel 1 (index0) resolves raceme attachment. The old roadside stand index4 is useful habitat only. Count branches of a SINGLE pictured panicle, not two crossed flowering heads.
tiles.short: On ONE complete flowering culm, count often 10–20 slender unilateral racemes.
tiles.status: WHOLE LIVE FLOWERING TUFT AND FULL ATTACHED HEAD PHOTOGRAPHED

tiles.heading: 02 · TRUE MEMBRANOUS LIGULE
tiles.details: Paspalum urvillei has a true, small FREE INNER membranous ligule (published approximately 3–5 mm in local-used treatments). Three NEW species-verified Harry Rose photographs show OUTER red/purple basal sheaths and long surface hairs, plus photo index7 which actually attaches roots. None exposes the adaxial blade/sheath junction with the free membrane. The earlier node photo is a hairy STEM NODE, also NOT the ligule. Score collar/sheath role only PARTIAL 0.5; seek one authenticated opened collar photo with 1-mm ruler.
tiles.short: Open the INNER blade–sheath collar: true membrane often 3–5 mm.
tiles.status: THREE REAL BASAL SHEATH PHOTOS — INNER TRUE MEMBRANE NOT YET PHOTOGRAPHED

tiles.heading: 03 · PAIRED RIPE SPIKELETS
tiles.details: Each small oval spikelet contains one lower sterile and one upper fertile floret; two adjacent spikelets are NOT two florets. Inspect at least five ripe pairs on the same raceme at 10–20× with a 1-mm ruler. Panel 3 shows actual attached spikelets but does not independently establish their size.
tiles.short: Paired, dorsally flattened spikelets usually about 2–2.8 mm long.
tiles.status: REAL SPIKELET PHOTO — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO CALIBRATED PAIRS

tiles.heading: 04 · GLUME, STERILE LEMMA, FERTILE LEMMA
tiles.details: The upper glume is thin, usually 3-veined, and has silky marginal hairs. The lower sterile lemma is similarly thin and can also be hairy; the upper fertile lemma is firm, pale and approximately 1.4–2.6 mm in AusGrass. A source-photographer-annotated reproductive panel labels real organs, but no millimeter ruler is present. Never invent a lower-glume arrow.
tiles.short: Lower glume absent; upper glume and sterile lemma silky-edged; firm fertile lemma inside.
tiles.status: REAL SOURCE-ANNOTATED PARTS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO MEASURED DISSECTION

tiles.heading: 05 · NO LONG AWN; DALLISGRASS LOOK-ALIKE
tiles.details: Vaseygrass spikelets commonly measure 2–2.8 mm; Paspalum dilatatum often about 2.7–3.9 mm. These ranges overlap. Compare a full flowering head, measured mature paired spikelets, hairy upper-glume margin and actual collar. Panel 6 is DALLISGRASS, a different species. Johnsongrass instead has a branching panicle with different paired-spikelet architecture. Newly linked gallery panel 11 (index10) is DIFFERENT native-regional *P. floridanum*, two authentic green racemes, CC BY-SA4 David Stang source. Keep both Vaseygrass and Dallisgrass look-alike cues and favor mature scale-matched spikelets rather than classifying all Paspalum as introduced.
tiles.short: Silky glume hairs are NOT awns; dallisgrass often has fewer racemes and larger spikelets.
tiles.status: REAL DALLISGRASS AND REGIONAL NATIVE FLORIDA PASPALUM COMPARISONS; MATCHED MICROSCOPY OPEN

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE / PHOTO AND SITE QA
tiles.details: CURRENT VERIFIED EVIDENCE: 9 physical exact species JPEGs (six new Harry Rose CC BY2), 11 total learner gallery panels (nine target species photos + different P. dilatatum and P. floridanum comparisons), with both old remote habitat/node references now LOCAL. Genuine photographed whole live flowering tuft, connected fibrous crown, outer basal sheaths, entire many-raceme flowering head and photographer-annotated upper glume/sterile/fertile lemma+palea. MAIN REMAINING ABOVEGROUND: physically OPENED INNER 3–5 mm triangular membranous ligule with 1-mm bar and same-scale actual mature Vasey vs Dallis spikelet pair. Older copyright/rights retained; live Pages/mobile not verified.
tiles.short: 9 archived Vaseygrass photos plus native/exotic comparison panels; true inner ligule and measured spikelets still missing
tiles.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — SIX-ROLE TARGET PASSED, LIGULE/PHOTO DEPLOY QA OPEN

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: VASEYGRASS (*Paspalum urvillei*) — now use PHOTO 10 of living leafy clump with many attached one-sided racemes, and PHOTO 8 of ACTUAL lifted purple-sheathed crown WITH connected fibrous roots. NEW PHOTO 7/9 show purple basal sheath long EXTERIOR hairs, NOT a true inner ligule. Exact FREE INNER membranous ligule (usually ~3–5 mm) remains unphotographed. Photo 2 is Harry Rose's REAL identified glume/sterile lemma/fertile lemma/palea dissection, and photo 3 real attached spikelets. Compare original Dallisgrass and newly added native regional Florida paspalum cross-taxon panels, without inferring Hays County nativity from their overseas/garden photos.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Look at SAME species gallery panel 10 (index9) for true healthy leafy tuft with flowering panicle on connected stems in field. The roadside scene in panel 5 (index4) is a population view, not an isolated plant.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Paspalum urvillei has a true, small FREE INNER membranous ligule (published approximately 3–5 mm in local-used treatments). Three NEW species-verified Harry Rose photographs show OUTER red/purple basal sheaths and long surface hairs, plus photo index7 which actually attaches roots. None exposes the adaxial blade/sheath junction with the free membrane. The earlier node photo is a hairy STEM NODE, also NOT the ligule. Score collar/sheath role only PARTIAL 0.5; seek one authenticated opened collar photo with 1-mm ruler.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: New Harry Rose locally archived gallery panel 10 (index9) documents a REAL leafy Vaseygrass clump with attached many-raceme flowering culms. Original whole-head panel 1 (index0) resolves raceme attachment. The old roadside stand index4 is useful habitat only. Count branches of a SINGLE pictured panicle, not two crossed flowering heads.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Count branches on ONE complete culm, not overlapping heads. Contrast 2–3 mm spikelets under measured macro with 3–4 mm long-haired dallisgrass; do not key solely by abundance of racemes or overall height. Use Florida paspalum as another few-branch, large-spikelet look-alike.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: VASEYGRASS — true separated floret parts, original photographer's labels
panels.caption: Read the labels ALREADY PRINTED by photographer Harry Rose on these dissected P. urvillei spikelets. IMPORTANT: the source explicitly states the LOWER GLUME IS MISSING in this pictured dissection; do not point to or teach a lower glume here. The upper glume and lower sterile lemma are similar in texture and length, while the upper fertile lemma and palea are shinier and harder. Dark feathery structures are stigmas, NOT awns. The source describes 2–2.5 mm spikelets, but this image has NO calibrated millimeter ruler; measure a separate specimen before confirming size.

This image is not a calibrated glume/lemma dissection: do not identify individual glumes, sterile/fertile lemmas or awn insertion points from this view. A measured mature same-plant specimen is still required.

intro: VASEYGRASS (*Paspalum urvillei*) — now use PHOTO 10 of living leafy clump with many attached one-sided racemes, and PHOTO 8 of ACTUAL lifted purple-sheathed crown WITH connected fibrous roots. NEW PHOTO 7/9 show purple basal sheath long EXTERIOR hairs, NOT a true inner ligule. Exact FREE INNER membranous ligule (usually ~3–5 mm) remains unphotographed. Photo 2 is Harry Rose's REAL identified glume/sterile lemma/fertile lemma/palea dissection, and photo 3 real attached spikelets. Compare original Dallisgrass and newly added native regional Florida paspalum cross-taxon panels, without inferring Hays County nativity from their overseas/garden photos.
memory_rule: COUNT COMPLETE RACEMES → MEASURE 5 RIPE SPIKELETS → CHECK MARGINAL HAIRS → ROOTED BASE/COLLAR. DALLIS few large silky; VASEY many small silky; FLORIDA few big round; PUBIFLORUM smaller oval; SETACEUM narrow variable; DISTICHUM two + real stolons.
safety_note: 11 gallery panels = nine exact source *P. urvillei* local JPEGs plus one *P. dilatatum* and one *P. floridanum* look-alike, both separately identified different species. No actual true inner ligule photo, no same-scale ripe comparison. No local Hays specimen from Australian photo.
field_rule: Use whole plant+flowering stalk+authentic rooted fibrous crown, paired mature spikelets and REAL glume parts; only call the ligule visible when it is the opened inner blade-sheath membrane, not basal sheath hairs or a hairy node.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Count branches on ONE complete culm, not overlapping heads. Contrast 2–3 mm spikelets under measured macro with 3–4 mm long-haired dallisgrass; do not key solely by abundance of racemes or overall height. Use Florida paspalum as another few-branch, large-spikelet look-alike.
